The same was not true for bone and muscle. For example, removal of either calcium, sodium or phosphate resulted in an inability to form bone, the infused mixture instead being directed to fat stores. Potassium was also shown to be essential for the retention of sodium and phosphate. Bodily retention of sodium and phosphate reverted ‘towards zero’ when potassium was withdrawn, demonstrating the essentiality of potassium for building tissues requiring sodium and phosphate. Likewise, withdrawal of sodium impaired the retention of nitrogen, phosphate and potassium by 2/3, and preventing calcium retention completely. This demonstrates the impact a low sodium diet might have on both bone and muscle, as has been found by the Women’s Health Initiative trial, which found low sodium intakes to be associated with osteoporosis . 

Further support for the concept that nutrient deficient diets may lead to the redirection of ingested nutrients and energy away from lean tissues in favour of adipose tissue has been provided by a double blind randomised controlled trial published in 2015 . Like much important research, it hasn’t received any where near the attention it deserves. 63 adults were randomised to receive either a placebo or a phosphate supplement. Not only did the subjects receiving the phosphate lose weight, their waist circumference also reduced indicating likely fat loss. 

Processed foods tend to be deficient in nutrients (unless they are specifically fortified, which is a somewhat tacit admission of their deficient state). This obvious poses issues for those consuming high processed food diets. The problem is however, even those making an effort to eat ‘real food’ are likely to not be ingesting as many nutrients as in generations gone by. Historical comparisons reveal a significant decline in the nutrient content of crops over recent decades. A landmark 2004 study analysed USDA data for 43 garden crops from 1950 to 1999, finding declines in several nutrients (protein, calcium, phosphorus, iron, riboflavin and ascorbic acid). The median declines ranged from 5% to 40%. More on this in another post. 

Ghrelin – the ‘ hunger hormone’ 
Another key hormone influencing our energy intake is ghrelin. Produced mainly in the stomach, with smaller amounts released by the small intestine, pancreas and brain, ghrelin signals that it is time to eat. When the stomach is empty, ghrelin production is typically at its highest. Importantly however, not all foods suppress ghrelin levels equally. Protein has the strongest suppressant effect on ghrelin, followed by carbohydrates and fat . This explains why protein rich meals typically result in feeling fuller, for longer. 

Food Processing and GLP-1
Energy intake and expenditure is also influenced by the digestability of food itself. Processing food, such as by grinding, milling or juicing, can increase how quickly it is absorbed, limiting the distance it travels along the intestines. This can influence key hormones responses regulating appetite and energy expenditure, as has been elegantly presented by Hungarian food scientist Gabor Erdosi in lectures available online. 

One key hormone influenced by food processing is Glucagon-like Peptide-1 (GLP-1). GLP-1 release suppresses the secretion of the hunger hormone, ghrelin, thereby suppressing hunger. 

GLP-1 itself is secreted by L-cells in the lower small intestine in response to the presence of carbohydrate, protein and fat. The location of L-cells far down the small intestine is significant, as rapidly digested foods may not reach this far. Consequently, foods which are rapidly absorbed as a consequence of processing, may not stimulate an appropriate increase in GLP-1 levels . This explains why you can often continue to eat copious amounts of processed foods without ever really getting a sense of true satiety.$$$

$$$ Hormonal effects also explain how gastric bypass surgery can result in weight loss – bypassing the upper stomach results in reduced levels of ghrelin, while bypassing the upper small intestine leads to increase nutrient delivery to the L-cells, enhancing GLP-1 secretion).  

***as an aside, cooking has also been shown to impact energy balance on meat diets. While cooking has been generally considered to have little impact on the energetic value of meat, it may influence satiety. A 2011 study fed an omniviorous species of mice known to consume both meat and starch (Mus musculus) diets consisting of either meat or sweet potato, both of which could be raw and whole, raw and pounded, cooked and whole or cooked and pounded . Interestingly, the greatest weight loss was found with raw sweet potato consumption, suggesting malabsorption. There was not weight loss at all in the cooked potato group.  Significantly, both categories of raw meat consumption were associated with about twice the degree of weight loss as compared to cooked meat consumption. Human studies will be needed to confirm whether this finding holds true for humans, however there are significant issues regarding food safety surrounding the consumption of raw meats).

This explains the profound appetite suppressing effects of Ozempic, remembering that GLP-1 profoundly inhibits the release of ghrelin, the ‘hunger hormone’. (Of course mucking around with human physiology rarely ends well > more on that in another article).

Glycaemic Index and GLP-1
The glycaemic index (GI) of a food is a measure of how quickly it raises blood sugar levels on a scale of 0-100, with 100 representing pure glucose. In other words, the glycaemic index is a surrogate for how quickly carbohydrate within a food can be digested. On this basis, high glycaemic index foods can be expected to result in an impaired GLP-1 response, therefore being less satiating. Furthermore, the solubility of starchy carbs correlates almost perfectly with the insulin response . One might consider then, that the glycaemic index would be a useful tool for assessing the potential hormonal impact of a food. This however, is only half correct- it is only true for starchy carbohydrates containing only glucose, and NOT fructose. 

Glycaemic index does not consider fructose
There is however, a major limitation of the glycaemic index which I suspect is deliberately overlooked by its advocates – it only considers glucose.  Sucrose (table sugar) and its various cousins (such as honey, brown sugar and syrups) contain fructose. Fructose is, by definition, ignored by the glycaemic index, which only measure the rise in blood glucose. This means the deleterious effects of fructose are entirely unaccounted for by the glycaemic index. Understand that fructose consumption is much more problematic than an equivalent amount of glucose, and you can see the issue. Not only is fructose about twice as sweet as glucose (making it more addictive), but it is about 8-10 times more reactive in terms of binding and chemically damaging, proteins (a process known as glycation). 

Glycaemic index in diabetes
While the GI gives some information regarding the rate that glucose enters the circulation, it is also true that all digested glucose will eventually reach the circulation. For diabetics who have trouble dealing with glucose in their blood, it is of little more than academic interest whether your sugar levels spike soon after a meal, or after a delay. The fact is, high blood glucose levels at any time are problematic. And this can be caused quite readily by low glycaemic index carbohydrates in diabetics. 

Further compounding this problem, is that when glucose levels get too high, some will be converted into fructose. One study found for example that 30% of all consumed glucose in diabetic subjects was converted into the more problematic fructose . Rather than glycaemic index then, diabetics ought to be more concerned about total carbohydrate (glucose) load. For example, while pumpkin has a high GI index of 75, it is only about 6% carbohydrate giving it is relatively small carbohydrate load, making it not an unreasonable choice for diabetics. 

(There is no readily available test to measure glycation damage by fructose. Both HbA1c and fructosamine only assess glycation by glucose).

Mechanism Behind Weight Loss

The weight-reducing effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists are attributed to their action on the hypothalamus, the brain’s appetite regulation center. By activating GLP-1 receptors in this region, these drugs promote a feeling of fullness and reduce appetite, leading to decreased caloric intake and subsequent weight loss. This mechanism was elucidated through detailed mapping of the human hypothalamus, enhancing our understanding of appetite control and paving the way for more targeted obesity treatments.  

Regulatory Approvals and Therapeutic Expansion

Recognizing their dual benefits, regulatory agencies expanded the indications for certain GLP-1 receptor agonists beyond diabetes management to include weight loss. For instance, in 2014, liraglutide was approved for weight management in individuals without diabetes.   Similarly, semaglutide received approval for chronic weight management in 2021, following clinical trials demonstrating its efficacy in inducing substantial weight loss.

Ongoing Research and Future Directions

The success of GLP-1 receptor agonists has spurred the development of next-generation weight-loss medications. Researchers are exploring combination therapies that not only enhance weight loss but also preserve muscle mass, addressing concerns about muscle depletion associated with weight reduction. Fen-Phen was a combination of two drugs, Fenfluramine and Phentermine, used as an appetite suppressant for weight loss in the 1990s. It gained popularity for its effectiveness in treating obesity. However, in 1997, the FDA banned Fenfluramine due to its severe cardiovascular side effects, especially heart valve damage. Phentermine is still available today as a weight loss medication.

2. DOSAGE (BEFORE BAN)

Fenfluramine: 20–40 mg per day

Phentermine: 15–37.5 mg per day

Taken together, they were believed to enhance weight loss effects by reducing appetite and increasing metabolism.

3. ADVANTAGES:

Rapid weight loss: Many users lost significant weight quickly.

Appetite suppression: Helped reduce calorie intake.

Increased metabolism: Boosted fat burning.

4. DISADVANTAGES:

Severe heart risks: Linked to heart valve damage.

Pulmonary hypertension: Increased risk of a rare but fatal lung condition.

Short-lived results: Weight regain was common after stopping.

Addiction potential: Phentermine is a stimulant with abuse potential.

5. SIDE EFFECTS:

Mild: Dry mouth, dizziness, constipation, insomnia, irritability.
Severe: Heart valve disease, high blood pressure, pulmonary hypertension, arrhythmias.

CURRENT STATUS:

Fenfluramine was banned due to safety concerns.

Phentermine is still available as a prescription weight loss drug.

Safer alternatives, such as Orlistat and GLP-1 receptor agonists (e.g., Semaglutide, Liraglutide), are now preferred for weight management.

---

## China’s Biotech Ascendancy: Catalysts and Capabilities  

### Workforce Development and Reverse Brain Drain  
A critical driver of China’s biotech surge is the repatriation of scientists trained at leading Western institutions. Over the past decade, government initiatives like the "Thousand Talents Plan" have incentivized researchers to return, establishing thriving biotech clusters in Shanghai, Beijing, and Shenzhen[6][17]. These professionals bring expertise in cutting-edge areas such as immunotherapy and antibody-drug conjugates, enabling Chinese firms to leapfrog traditional R&D timelines. For instance, Akeso’s PD-1/VEGF bispecific antibody—licensed to Summit Therapeutics—was developed by a team led by U.S.-educated researchers who streamlined preclinical testing from 18 months to just 9[3][6]. This "scrappy" approach, leveraging lower labor costs (30–50% less than U.S. equivalents) and high-risk tolerance, has allowed China to compress drug discovery cycles by 40% compared to Western benchmarks[17].  

### Regulatory Reforms Accelerating Innovation  
China’s 2015 drug regulatory overhaul marked a turning point, aligning approval processes with international standards while slashing clinical trial application timelines from 31 months to 2 months[17]. The National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) now grants conditional approvals for breakthrough therapies based on Phase II data, a stark contrast to the FDA’s more conservative stance. Additionally, the rise of investigator-initiated trials (IITs)—which increased from 2,500 in 2018 to over 8,000 in 2024—has enabled rapid proof-of-concept studies in areas like CAR-T cell therapy[3]. However, laxer ethical oversight in some IITs has raised concerns; a 2024 study found that 23% of participants in Shanghai trials were inadequately informed about alternative treatments[3].

China’s vast patient population and centralized healthcare system provide unparalleled advantages in clinical recruitment. For example, Hansoh Pharma enrolled 1,200 NSCLC patients for its oral GLP-1 trial in just 8 months—a process that typically takes 18–24 months in the U.S.—by leveraging partnerships with 60+ tier-3 hospitals[4][16]. Per-patient trial costs average $15,000 in China versus $75,000 in the U.S., driven by lower institutional review board fees and waived overhead charges at public hospitals[3][6]. This scalability extends to manufacturing: WuXi Biologics offers antibody production at $150/gram compared to $500/gram in the West, making China the global leader in biosimilar production[16].

- **Enhance Collaboration**: Create neutral-ground R&D hubs in Singapore or Dubai to circumvent geopolitical barriers

China’s biotech ascendancy represents both opportunity and disruption. Patients stand to benefit from accelerated access to affordable therapies, with Chinese-developed drugs projected to reduce global oncology treatment costs by 25% by 2030[17]. However, the U.S. and EU must balance openness with strategic investments in core competencies like AI-driven drug discovery and advanced manufacturing. Could obesity drugs help with alcohol cravings? New study suggests potential

By CARLA K. JOHNSON
Medications that have transformed the treatment of obesity may also help people drink less alcohol, according to new government-funded research.
The study was small — just 48 adults — and lasted just over two months, so it’s not the final word. Experts say it’s not yet clear how safe these drugs are for people who don’t need to lose weight.
But the results add to evidence from animal studies and reports that people are finding drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy helpful to manage cravings, not just for food, but also for tobacco and alcohol. Scientists are studying these drugs in smokers, people with opioid addiction and cocaine users.
“This is such promising data. And we need more of it,” said study co-author Dr. Klara Klein, of the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, who treats patients with diabetes and obesity. “We frequently will hear that once people start these medications that their desire to drink is very reduced, if not completely abolished."
The drugs, known as GLP-1 receptor agonists, work by mimicking hormones in the gut and the brain to regulate appetite and feelings of fullness. The new study looked at one of these drugs, semaglutide, which is the drug in Ozempic and Wegovy.
The research, published Wednesday in the journal JAMA Psychiatry, was funded by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, part of the National Institutes of Health.
There are already three medications approved to treat alcohol use disorder, so until larger studies can confirm the findings, people should talk to their doctor about what's already available, said lead author Christian Hendershot, an addiction researcher at University of Southern California.
For the new study, researchers recruited people who reported symptoms of alcohol use disorder, such as difficulty controlling their drinking, but weren’t actively seeking treatment for it.
First, each person came to a lab where they were served their favorite alcoholic beverage and could drink as much as they wanted over two hours.
Then, researchers randomly assigned half the people to get a weekly injection of semaglutide. The other half got sham injections.
For nine weeks, everyone kept track of their drinking habits and their desire for alcohol. A lab visit with their favorite alcohol was repeated at the end of the study.
During the last weeks of the study, nearly 40% in the semaglutide group reported no heavy drinking days compared with 20% in the placebo group. And in the final lab test, the semaglutide group drank roughly half the amount, on average, compared to those who got the placebo.
Everyone in the study was overweight. It's unclear how safe the drugs would be for a person of normal weight, Klein said.
Smokers in the study who got the semaglutide also cut back on cigarettes, noted Luba Yammine of UTHealth Houston, who is leading other research on GLP-1 drugs for people who want to quit smoking. The finding is promising but more data is needed, Yammine said.
The study “provides additional important information on the potential role of this new class of medications” in treating certain addictions, said Dr. Lorenzo Leggio, an NIH researcher who is leading a 20-week trial of semaglutide for alcohol use disorder now underway in Baltimore.
“It is important to keep in mind that we need larger randomized clinical trials to confirm these findings,” Leggio said.

Ozempic (semaglutide) is a medication primarily used for managing type 2 diabetes, though it has also gained attention for its weight loss effects. Here are some of the side effects associated with Ozempic, based on available information:

Common Side Effects:
Gastrointestinal Issues:
Nausea: Often the most reported side effect, especially when starting the medication or increasing the dose.
Vomiting, Diarrhea, Stomach Pain, and Constipation are also frequently noted.
Other Mild Side Effects:
Fatigue
Dizziness
Headaches
Heartburn or Acid Reflux
Burping
Loss of Appetite
Serious Side Effects:
Hypoglycemia (Low Blood Sugar): More common when Ozempic is used with other diabetes medications like insulin or sulfonylureas.
Pancreatitis: Inflammation of the pancreas, which can cause severe abdominal pain.
Gallbladder Problems: Including the formation of gallstones or gallbladder inflammation.
Vision Changes: Particularly in those with diabetic retinopathy, where rapid blood sugar control can temporarily worsen eye conditions.
Kidney Problems: Including acute kidney injury, especially if dehydration occurs due to gastrointestinal side effects.
Ileus: Also known as stomach paralysis, where food does not move through the intestines properly.
Thyroid Tumors: Ozempic has a boxed warning for the risk of thyroid C-cell tumors, observed in animal studies, though it's not clear if it increases this risk in humans.

Allergic Reactions: Including severe reactions that might require immediate medical attention.
Additional Considerations:
Ozempic Face: Rapid weight loss can lead to noticeable changes in facial appearance, such as sagging skin or wrinkles.
Long-term Effects: While most side effects are short-term, long-term effects on organs like the pancreas, kidneys, or thyroid are still under study. The drug has been on the market for less than 10 years, so long-term data is limited.
Management:
For nausea or gastrointestinal issues, taking Ozempic with food, eating smaller meals more frequently, staying hydrated, and possibly adjusting the dose under medical supervision can help.
Regular monitoring by a healthcare provider is crucial, especially for those with pre-existing conditions that could be exacerbated by Ozempic's side effects.
It's important for anyone considering or using Ozempic to discuss these potential side effects with their healthcare provider, as individual responses to the medication can vary. They should also be aware of any new or worsening symptoms and report these promptly.

A podcast by the ever-popular Oprah Winfrey — where she interviewed endocrinologist Dr Ania Jastreboff from Yale University — emphasised the concept of #obesity as a disease. A recent Lancet commission report on obesity also said the same. Just to put the record straight, the WHO classified obesity as a disease in 1997. In fact, not only is it a disease like diabetes or hypertension, it is also the mother of most chronic diseases, requiring lifelong management.

The word “obesity” carries a stigma and it can be highly demotivating for an individual to be labelled obese or morbidly obese, terms that are widely used. A reasonable suggestion by the American Association of Endocrinologists, which we have adopted, is the acronym ABCD — Adiposity Based Chronic Disease.

Regardless of the semantics, we have to think of obesity as a chronic “neuroendocrine” disease — a disturbance of the hormone-brain axis. When we eat, the intestines send out signals (like the GLP1 hormone) to the pancreas and other parts of the body, including the brain. The brain tells us when we are satiated and should stop eating. Brain centres, under the influence of brain hormones, also control our appetite. Putting it simply, dysregulation of this hormone-brain axis leads to a mismatch between our requirements and what we eat. As a result, we eat excessively and put on weight. This axis determines the set point for weight and is different for every individual. Very often, therefore, it is not the individual’s fault that they tend to gain weight more easily than their peers, or lose less weight than others on medication.

If we think of obesity as a disease, we will have little problem in accepting that it should be treated with medication. There is no reason for feeling guilty or ashamed about the use of medication to treat obesity. It is not a sign of defeat. We need to think of obesity in the same way as we think of other chronic diseases like diabetes, blood pressure and high cholesterol. The new class of GLP1 drugs typified by semaglutide (#ozempic , #Wegovy) and tirzepatide (#Mounjaro, #Zepbound) — and a whole bunch of new ones in development — at least partially treats the biological defect in the brain that causes obesity. By resetting the set point, they help us lower weight. However, as with most medications, they work only as long as they are used. Once off the drug, the weight can come back. It is very important to set realistic targets when initiating therapy. The target cannot always be what the patient desires. A conversation about this between patient and doctor is essential. While obesity is a disease, it cannot be treated just by medication. This axis determines the set point for weight and is different for every individual. Very often, therefore, it is not the individual’s fault that they tend to gain weight more easily than their peers, or lose less weight than others on medication.

If we think of obesity as a disease, we will have little problem in accepting that it should be treated with medication. There is no reason for feeling guilty or ashamed about the use of medication to treat obesity. It is not a sign of defeat. We need to think of obesity in the same way as we think of other chronic diseases like diabetes, blood pressure and high cholesterol. The new class of GLP1 drugs typified by semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbould) — and a whole bunch of new ones in development — at least partially treats the biological defect in the brain that causes obesity. By resetting the set point, they help us lower weight. However, as with most medications, they work only as long as they are used. Once off the drug, the weight can come back. The method for dose adjustment that I use is similar to that discussed by Dr Jastreboff. The principle is to start low and increase slowly, to reduce side effects. When target weight has been achieved or weight has plateaued at the maximum tolerated dose, I try to continue the patient on the lowest possible maintenance dose.

It is very important to set realistic targets when initiating therapy. The target cannot always be what the patient desires. A conversation about this between patient and doctor is essential. For someone who is 5’8” and weighs 120 kg, to aim for an ideal body weight of 70 kg is virtually impossible. It is important not to be driven by cosmetic considerations alone. Many individuals have body image issues — I get requests from women who are underweight but want to lose more weight for a modelling assignment or a wedding. It is also important for potential users to realise that not everyone loses huge amounts of weight.

While obesity is a disease, it cannot be treated just by medication. One can never ignore that treating obesity involves a lot of effort on the individual’s part, and lifestyle measures remain the foundation of successful management — in the same way as for diabetes. I have some patients who tend to depend solely on medication and stop making any lifestyle effort. Such patients are bound to be long-term failures as they will gain weight rapidly whenever they try to reduce the medication dose.

There was not much discussion about side effects in the Oprah interview, but I would like to point out some. Gastro-intestinal side effects are common and usually manageable. Pancreatitis is exceedingly rare. Muscle loss that occurs due to rapid weight loss, although not a direct drug effect, is of particular concern among Indians who often have low muscle mass to start with. The recent report of the rare occurrence of eye optic neuropathy (NIAON) with the use of semaglutide tells us that continued pharmacovigilance is required. And while it is true that most patients with obesity require continued treatment, I would be cautious in recommending lifelong treatment with the new GLP1 drugs for every obese individual till more data emerges.

Obesity is associated with absenteeism, presenteeism, and reduced workforce participation. If more individuals remain healthy enough to participate in the workforce, labor supply could expand, slightly moderating wage growth. United States
The US currently leads in both obesity rates and early adoption of GLP-1 medications for weight loss. In this note for my patients, I detail the evidence that clearly demonstrates this is not a drug to be taken lightly. If you know anyone prescribing Ozempic, they should read this. 

Ozempic - a disaster waiting to happen
Glucagon-like Peptide-1 (GLP-1) is a key hormone regulating energy balance. It's release can be heavily influenced by processing of food, such as grinding, milling, or juicing, which can increase how quickly it is absorbed.

One key mechanism of GLP-1 is to suppress secretion of the hunger hormone, ghrelin, thereby suppressing hunger. GLP-1 itself is secreted by L-cells in the lower small intestine in response to the presence of nutrients incluiding carbohydrate, protein, and fat. The location of L-cells far down the small intestine is significant, as rapidly digested processed foods may not reach this far. Consequently processed foods may not stimulate an appropriate increase in GLP-1 levels, leading to persistently high ghrelin levels and hunger. This explains why one can often continue consuming large amounts of processed foods without experiencing true satiety.

Ozempic (Semaglutide) mimics the effects of natural GLP-1 but has a longer duration of action, explaining its profound appetite-suppressing effects.  However, mucking around with human physiology can often have unintended consequences.

One of the trials used for the approval of Ozempic was a a drug company-funded trial known as STEP1. It demonstrated impressive weight loss over 68 weeks of once-weekly injections, the more than 1,300 participants experiencing an average weight loss of 16.86 kg (37lbs). As always however, the devil is in the detail. DEXA body composition scanning was performed on 95 of the STEP1 subjects, and revealed first of all that less than 5% of fat lost was the more problematic visceral fat. Even more concerning, 41% of the total weight lost appeared to come from muscle and bone. You read that correctly. These subjects were on a path both to osteoporosis and sarcopenia (excessive muscle loss).

This obvious raises questions about the impact of Ozempic on bone health. A double-blinded, randomised controlled trial was subsequently conducted at two public hospitals in Denmark. This study also found impairment in bone health, weekly semaglutide injections over 52 weeks resulting in bone mass loss in the lumbar spine and hip, as well as thinning of the outer strong cortical bone of the tibia. Perhaps even more concerningly however was that levels of the bone resorption marker C-terminal telopeptide (CTX) continued to rise throughout the study. This suggests that not only is bone loss ongoing while taking semaglutide, but the rate of bone loss may even accelerate with prolonged used. I cannot emphasise this enough. The longer subjects take semaglutide, the closer to osteoporosis they likely get.

Which then raises the question of what happens when semaglutide is ceased? Does bone mass return. Unfortunately we don't know the answer to this question, because the drug company funded follow-up to the STEP1 trial, which followed subjects for 12 months after discontinuing semaglutide only reported on weight, not body composition. Still even looking only at weight, the results were not good. Participants regained on average two-thirds of the weight they had lost. Given that 59% of the initial weight loss was fat, it is plausible that the regained weight was primarily composed of fat. It is perhaps unlikely that if indeed these subjects had only regained muscle and bone, that we would not have been told about it.

Additionally, the STEP1 trial found treatment with semaglutide to be associated with significant increases in the pancreatic enzyme lipase (rising from 25 U/L to 36 U/L). This is concerning given that Roche withdrew another GLP-1 agonist, Taspoglutide, due to severe side effects, including pancreatitis. Similarly, Exenatide (Byetta), another drug in this class, carries a black box warning for both pancreatitis and kidney dysfunction.

There are of course other issues with this class of drug, however I think these alone justify severe caution be used when prescribing it. The fact is, it is very likely that the longer you are on this drug, the weaker your bones get. And with no evidence that this bone mass returns when it is stopped, we may well be facing a future tsunami of premature osteoporosis and sacropenia in coming years.

Exendin-4: This is a protein found in the Gila monster's venom, which has a structure and function similar to human GLP-1 but with a significantly longer duration of action. Exendin-4 was the first venom-derived peptide used in the development of anti-diabetic medication.

Exenatide: The first drug developed from this research was Byetta (exenatide), which is a synthetic version of exendin-4. Byetta was approved for the treatment of type 2 diabetes because it mimics the effects of GLP-1, promoting insulin secretion, slowing gastric emptying, and reducing appetite.

Semaglutide (Ozempic): Although not directly derived from venom, the concept and mechanism of action of semaglutide were heavily influenced by the findings from exendin-4. Semaglutide is a human GLP-1 analog designed to have similar benefits but with modifications for longer-lasting effects and better patient compliance (weekly injections versus multiple daily doses for some other GLP-1 agonists).

So while Ozempic itself isn't directly "derived" from venom in the sense of being an extract or direct copy, its development was inspired by and built upon the discovery of exendin-4 in Gila monster venom. This represents a fascinating example of how nature can inform drug development, with venom compounds providing a blueprint for creating synthetic analogs for therapeutic use.

General Use and Approval:
Primary Use: Ozempic is FDA-approved for managing blood sugar levels in adults with type 2 diabetes (T2DM) and for reducing the risk of major cardiovascular events in those with T2DM and known heart disease.

Off-label Use: It's also used off-label for weight loss, although its sibling drug, Wegovy, is approved specifically for chronic weight management.

Common Side Effects:
Gastrointestinal Issues: The most frequently reported side effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and constipation. These are usually mild to moderate and tend to improve over time.

Appetite and Weight: Ozempic can reduce appetite, leading to weight loss. However, this effect is not consistent across all users, and weight regain can occur once the medication is discontinued.

Serious Side Effects:
Thyroid Tumors/Cancer: There's a boxed warning for the potential risk of thyroid C-cell tumors, including medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), based on animal studies. It's not clear if this applies to humans, but individuals with a personal or family history of MTC or MEN 2 should avoid Ozempic.

Pancreatitis: There have been reports of pancreatitis, which can be severe. Symptoms include severe abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting.

Kidney Problems: Acute kidney injury and worsening of pre-existing kidney disease have been observed. Dehydration from gastrointestinal side effects can exacerbate these risks.

Gallbladder Issues: Increased risks of gallbladder disease, including gallstones and cholecystitis, have been noted.

Hypoglycemia: Particularly when used with insulin or sulfonylureas, there's an increased risk of low blood sugar.

Vision Changes: Rapid changes in blood sugar control can temporarily worsen diabetic retinopathy, a condition affecting the eyes.

Allergic Reactions: Including angioedema, which can be life-threatening, requiring immediate medical attention.

Ileus (Intestinal Blockage): There have been reports of ileus, which is a condition where the intestines do not move contents through normally, leading to potential blockages.

Mental Health: Some posts on X have raised concerns about increased risks of depression, anxiety, and suicidal behavior linked to GLP-1 agonists like Ozempic, though these are not universally accepted or confirmed in all studies.

Long-term Effects:
Muscle and Bone Loss: Weight loss can include a significant loss of muscle mass, which might affect health and appearance long-term.

Dependence on Drug: There's an implication that discontinuing Ozempic might lead to weight regain, suggesting a potential long-term dependency for weight management.

Benefits:
Cardiovascular Protection: Studies suggest Ozempic can reduce the risk of cardiovascular events like heart attacks or strokes, independent of weight loss.
Kidney Health: Some research indicates potential protective effects on kidney function, particularly in those with T2DM.

Considerations:
Cost and Accessibility: The cost can be prohibitive out-of-pocket, though insurance coverage for diabetes might apply. For weight loss, coverage might be less consistent.

Monitoring and Management: Regular monitoring by healthcare providers is essential due to the range of side effects and the need for dosage adjustments.

The Satiety Solution: Understanding Fullness, Obesity Trends, and the Role of Weight Loss Medications

Over the past seven decades, obesity rates in the United States have escalated dramatically. In the early 1960s, approximately 13% of adults were classified as obese. By 2017–2018, this figure had risen to 42.4%, with severe obesity reaching 9.2%  . This surge is attributed to various factors, including dietary changes, reduced physical activity, and increased consumption of processed foods.

Understanding Satiety and Its Primary Drivers

Satiety, the sensation of fullness that signals us to stop eating, is influenced by several key dietary components:
1.Saturated Fats: These fats slow gastric emptying and stimulate the release of hormones like cholecystokinin (CCK) and peptide YY (PYY), which signal fullness to the brain. Their energy density also provides a prolonged feeling of fullness after consumption.
2.Proteins: Protein is highly satiating, promoting the release of hormones such as GLP-1 and PYY, which reduce hunger. It also suppresses ghrelin, the “hunger hormone,” leading to prolonged satiety.
3.Minerals: Adequate intake of minerals like magnesium, calcium, and zinc is essential for metabolic functions and appetite regulation. Deficiencies can disrupt these processes, leading to increased hunger and cravings.

Weight Loss Medications: GLP-1 Agonists and Appetite Suppressants

In response to rising obesity rates, various weight loss medications have been developed, primarily focusing on appetite suppression and enhancing satiety. Among these, GLP-1 receptor agonists have gained prominence.

GLP-1 Receptor Agonists

Originally developed for type 2 diabetes management, GLP-1 receptor agonists, such as semaglutide (marketed as Ozempic and Wegovy), have demonstrated significant weight loss effects. They mimic the GLP-1 hormone, enhancing insulin secretion, slowing gastric emptying, and promoting satiety.

Efficacy: Clinical trials have shown that semaglutide can lead to substantial weight loss. For instance, participants using semaglutide experienced significant reductions in body weight compared to those on a placebo.

Side Effects: Common side effects include gastrointestinal issues such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea,  constipation as well as Pancreatitis [inflammation of the pancreas which can be life threatening if not recognized appropriately and GLP-1 cessation occurs]. Some users have reported facial changes due to rapid weight loss, often referred to as “Ozempic face”.

Traditional appetite suppressants, like phentermine, function by stimulating the central nervous system to reduce hunger.

Efficacy: These medications can lead to short-term weight loss; however, their effectiveness often diminishes over time, and they are typically approved for short-term use.

Side Effects: Potential side effects include increased heart rate, elevated blood pressure, insomnia, dizziness, and mood changes.

Comparative Insights and Long-Term Success

While both GLP-1 agonists and traditional appetite suppressants aim to reduce hunger and promote weight loss, GLP-1 agonists offer a more physiological approach by mimicking natural satiety hormones. However, individual responses vary, and not all users experience significant weight loss. Some individuals may not respond to these medications, highlighting the need for personalized treatment plans .

Active Ingredients:
Ozempic contains semaglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist.
Mounjaro contains tirzepatide, which is a dual agonist for both GLP-1 and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptors.

Mechanism of Action:
Ozempic works by mimicking the GLP-1 hormone, which helps reduce blood sugar levels by increasing insulin secretion, slowing gastric emptying, and reducing appetite.
Mounjaro not only mimics GLP-1 but also GIP. This dual action leads to enhanced control over blood sugar levels, potentially offering greater reductions in A1C (a measure of average blood glucose over two to three months) and more significant weight loss compared to medications that only target GLP-1.

Efficacy for Weight Loss:
Both drugs have shown to aid in weight loss, but Mounjaro has been noted in various studies to potentially lead to more substantial weight reduction. A study published in JAMA Internal Medicine indicated that patients on Mounjaro lost significantly more weight than those on Ozempic, with a 15.3% average weight loss for Mounjaro compared to 8.3% for Ozempic after one year.📷

FDA Approvals and Uses:
Ozempic is approved for type 2 diabetes management and reducing the risk of major cardiovascular events in adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease.
Mounjaro is approved for type 2 diabetes. While not officially approved for weight loss in the U.S., it has been used off-label for this purpose, and in the UK, it's specifically approved for weight management.📷

Side Effects:
Both medications share common side effects...

Cardiovascular Benefits:
Ozempic has an additional FDA approval for reducing cardiovascular risk in certain diabetic patients, a benefit not yet officially recognized for Mounjaro, although studies are ongoing.📷

Summary
In summary, while both drugs are effective for managing blood sugar in type 2 diabetes, Mounjaro has shown a potential edge in weight loss efficacy due to its dual hormonal action. However, individual responses can vary, and side effect profiles might influence which medication is more suitable for a particular patient. Always consult with healthcare providers for personalized medical advice.

By Jason Gale
(Bloomberg) -- One of the world’s largest studies of
Ozempic, Mounjaro and other blockbuster diabetes and obesity
drugs highlighted their impact on the brain, pointing to
benefits from addiction to schizophrenia.
The research tracked the effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists
on diabetic US veterans for up to five years, making it one of
the most extensive so far on a class of medicines that includes
Novo Nordisk A/S’s Wegovy and Eli Lilly & Co.’s Zepbound.
The study, published Monday in the journal Nature Medicine,
found protective effects related to impulse control, adding to
evidence that the medicines may not only suppress appetite but
also help curb alcoholism and other addictions.
“These drugs are helping us uncover the real underpinnings
of obesity,” said co-author Ziyad Al-Aly, director of the
Clinical Epidemiology Center at the Veterans Affairs St. Louis
Health Care System.  
“Effectively treating obesity requires drugs that address
the root cause: addictive-like behavior toward food,” he said.
“This may explain why GLP-1s have been so spectacularly
successful as anti-obesity medicines, while many previous
treatments that didn’t target the addiction pathway have failed
miserably.”
The findings support ongoing research into the medicines’
potential for treating opioid- and cocaine-use disorders,
further broadening the scope of these drugs, which Bloomberg
Intelligence estimates will reap over $93 billion globally by
2030 for obesity alone.
Al-Aly’s earlier research mined the Veterans Affairs’
extensive databases to uncover links between prolonged use of
popular heartburn medications and kidney damage, as well as the
long-term health impacts of Covid-19. 
The latest study analyzed almost 216,000 patients taking
GLP-1s for a median of 3.7 years, examining associations with
175 health outcomes and comparing results to those of patients
on other diabetes drugs or receiving standard care for the
metabolic disorder.
The study is notable for examining a broad range of medical
conditions, said Christian Hendershot, director of clinical
research at the University of Southern California’s Institute
for Addiction Science in Los Angeles.
“It doesn’t prove anything about causality, as the authors
acknowledge, but it’s a nice starting point for narrowing in on
which classes of disorders we might want to study,” said
Hendershot, who is researching GLP-1s for addictions to nicotine
and alcohol.

Kidney Stones

The results consistently showed both benefits and risks
beyond those currently recognized, according to Al-Aly.
Drawbacks included an increased likelihood of drug-induced acute
pancreatitis or inflammation of the pancreas, low blood
pressure, fainting, arthritic conditions, and kidney stones.
On the benefits side, GLP-1s were linked to a reduced risk
of alcohol, cannabis, opioid, and stimulant-use disorders as
well as neurocognitive disorders such as Alzheimer’s and
dementia.
The study “provides an interesting analysis,” but its focus
on mostly white male veterans may limit how well the findings
apply to others, said Margaret Morris, an obesity expert and
professor of pharmacology at Sydney’s University of New South
Wales. 
Widespread use of GLP-1s, reported to be taken by as many
as 25 million American adults, could cut alcohol consumption in
the US by up to 29 million liters (7.7 million gallons) this
year, according to a report from BMI Country Risk & Industry
Research.

Suicide Risk

Initial concerns about suicidal thoughts among users led to
a review by the European Medicines Agency, which found no causal
link. Al-Aly’s study supports these findings and aligns with
research suggesting GLP-1s may have anti-depressive effects and
reduce the risk of intentional self-harm.
The results should offer reassurance about safety for
people with mental illness, said Dan Siskind, a professor of
psychiatry at the University of Queensland.

Let's discuss Semaglutide, known as Ozempic for diabetes or Wegovy for weight loss. It's a GLP-1 agonist, mimicking a hormone that regulates several bodily functions.

My Journey-

A few years ago, I unexpectedly ballooned from a size 4 to a size 20. Despite an active lifestyle (20k steps/day as an ER nurse) and a consistent diet, my weight only increased. I mean, I wasn’t just fluffy, I was unhealthily FAT! My primary care physician suggested the usual: more exercise, less food. Calories in vs calories out. She said it was just one of the things that happen as we “get older.”

I tried every diet- Keto, whole 30, Mediterranean. I added in intermittent fasting. I went to the gym on my days off. I’d lose 1-2 pounds, then I’d  gain 3 more. My doctor said I must be mistaken about my calories and exercise and to try harder. So I did. 

At the same time, I found out I have an autoimmune disease that will destroy my liver and the only cure is a transplant. So off I went to a transplant doctor. He tells me it’ll be hard to get me a liver because I’m too fat. But, he said he prescribe a newer diabetes medication to one of his patients and she lost a significant amount of weight so I said I’d try it. 

For 6 months I puked every single day, sometimes multiple times. I got headaches so bad that one time I thought I was having a stroke. My heartburn was so brutal that I couldn’t lay down at night. But, I didn’t lose a pound. Nope, not one!!

I went back to the transplant doctor who was disappointed, to say the least. He said we’d have to try something else. Then he did a quick ultrasound of my liver and was shocked. My super fatty liver had completely resolved! Even though I still wiggled like a bowl full of jello, my internal organs had shed the fat!! So he renewed my prescription and said he’d keep looking for something that would help with my weight. 

A week later, I noticed I was down 2 pounds. In fact, every week thereafter I lost 2-4 pounds! I was back to my size 4 within a year!!

So I decided to put my nursing degree to work and do a deep dive into how it work and why. 

Like I said, it’s a hormone. As we age or contract certain conditions, our hormones change and the GLP-1 seems to be the main culprit that many suddenly deplete. 

GLP-1 hormones are responsible for so many things! First, it slows gastric emptying, so the food stays in your stomach longer, making you full for longer. 

It also sends a signal to your brain when you’ve eaten enough that says, “You’re full!”  Without this hormone, you only stop eating because you know you should. 

Then, it sends a signal to your pancreas to tell it whether to burn the calories as instant energy, or store the calories as fat for future energy. If it doesn’t get the signal, your body thinks that the hormone is saying famine is coming and it better store every calorie it gets as fat. My body had literally been betraying me!!

It’s years later, and I’m still taking the maximum dose every week. If I miss a week or try to lower my dose, I’ll put 5 pounds on in 10 days. This is a life long medication that is correcting a medical hormonal deficiency. 

But it is NOT a magic shot. It has some pretty significant side effects for about 20% of those who take it (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, headache, heartburn, fatigue).  It can also cause DANGEROUS conditions that might kill you like pancreatitis, gallbladder attacks, bowel blockages, kidney damage, and stomach paralysis. Those are crazy rare, but they can happen, so you need to know what to look out for. 

But it is also being studied and has been shown to reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke, prevent Alzheimer’s, and cure or improve certain autoimmune diseases. 

To me, the benefits outweigh the risks. It’s a medication that changed my life, but it took a lot of time. What was right for me might not be for everyone, but now you know my story.

"I’m Kelly Grant, a health reporter at The Globe and Mail. I was intrigued when I saw that Health Canada approved Wegovy – a higher-dose version of the wildly popular diabetes drug Ozempic – for reducing the risk of heart attacks late last year.
I wondered what the approval might mean for Canada’s public drug plans. I wrote about that today in a story featuring a Toronto man who took part in the clinical trial that led to the cardiovascular approval. The 68-year-old trucker stopped taking Wegovy when the trial ended because he can’t afford it. Ontario’s drug benefit program doesn’t cover it.
You may not have heard of Wegovy, but you’ve definitely heard of Ozempic, the diabetes treatment with the earworm jingle (Oh-Oh-Oh-Ozempic!) and the capacity to make celebrities and regular humans thin. Wegovy and Ozempic are the same drug, semaglutide. Wegovy is simply sold at a higher dose and marketed for weight loss instead of diabetes.

I was interested in the cardiovascular authorization because of what it could mean for public coverage of Wegovy and other drugs that belong to a class called glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists. GLP-1 drugs are proving to be remarkable weight-loss aids for people who’ve struggled to shed pounds all their lives, but Canada’s provincial and territorial drug programs have generally refused to pay for them – or for any prescription drugs they consider cosmetic.
Could that change now that research shows semaglutide cuts the risk of heart attacks, strokes and death from cardiovascular causes by 20 per cent in people with pre-existing cardiovascular disease who are overweight or obese but who don’t have diabetes?
If trends in the United States and Europe are any guide, the answer will be yes. South of the border, Medicare and Medicaid didn’t start covering Wegovy until the Food and Drug Administration approved it for cardiovascular protection.

In a related development, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced just last week that they will pay for another GLP-1 drug, tirzepatide, sold as Zepbound, for obstructive sleep apnea. The FDA approved Zepbound for sleep apnea on Dec. 20.
In this country, the organization that sets the tone for public coverage of medications is called Canada’s Drug Agency, formerly the Canadian Agency for Drugs and Technologies in Health (CADTH).
In 2022, a CADTH expert committee advised public drug plans not to cover Wegovy for weight loss because, at the time, there wasn’t enough high-quality scientific evidence that semaglutide-induced weight loss improved other diseases associated with obesity.

Now, with positive clinical trials and the new Health Canada indication in hand, the Danish pharmaceutical giant Novo Nordisk confirmed to me that it has asked Canada’s Drug Agency to take a second look. A fresh verdict on Wegovy is expected later this year.
Tucked into CADTH’s dense 2022 report are some estimates of what it might cost to fund Wegovy for every Canadian who meets the Health Canada criteria for taking the drug, and who qualifies for a taxpayer-funded drug program. (Public plans differ from province to province, but they usually cover the old and the poor.)
Novo Nordisk submitted a three-year budget impact assessment of $1.06-billion; CADTH’s experts countered that the budget impact could be as high as $4-billion over three years, although both sides agreed it would be less if Wegovy were covered for a narrow subset of patients.

Predicting how new drugs might affect public health spending is always a challenge. Policy makers have to balance the upfront cost of prescriptions with the hope that keeping people healthy and out of hospital will save money in the future.
There are many complicating factors when it comes to judging the cost effectiveness of medications that are widely used or prohibitively expensive, not the least of which is the fact that real drug prices are often kept secret. Public payers routinely negotiate confidential discounts off the sticker price.
In the end, decision makers have to contend with a reality that Subodh Verma, a Toronto cardiac surgeon-scientist who helped lead several pivotal clinical trials of GLP-1 drugs for cardiovascular disease, put bluntly to me in an interview: “Saving lives costs money.”

Ozempic is a prescription medication used to improve blood sugar control in adults with type 2 diabetes. It contains the active ingredient semaglutide, which belongs to a class of drugs called GLP-1 receptor agonists. Ozempic can also help promote weight loss and is sometimes prescribed off-label for this purpose.

How Ozempic Works

Mimics GLP-1 Hormone: It mimics a natural hormone (GLP-1) that helps regulate blood sugar levels and appetite.

Reduces Blood Sugar: It stimulates insulin production and reduces glucose production in the liver when blood sugar is high.

Slows Digestion: Delays stomach emptying, which helps control appetite and reduce food intake, aiding in weight loss.

How to Use Ozempic

1. Administration:

Ozempic is injected subcutaneously (under the skin), typically once a week.

You can inject it in the abdomen, thigh, or upper arm.

2. Dosage:

The initial dose is usually 0.25 mg per week for 4 weeks, then increased to 0.5 mg per week. Your doctor might adjust the dose based on your response.

3. Timing:

Inject it on the same day each week, at any time, with or without food.

Who Can Use It?

Adults with type 2 diabetes who need better blood sugar control.

People seeking assistance with weight management (when prescribed off-label).

Side Effects

Common: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, decreased appetite.

Serious (rare): Pancreatitis, kidney issues, allergic reactions, or thyroid tumors.

Precautions

Not suitable for individuals with type 1 diabetes or diabetic ketoacidosis.

Avoid if you have a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma.

Inform your doctor about any other medications, as Ozempic can interact with them.

If you're considering Ozempic, consult your doctor for personalized advice on its suitability and proper use.

From nausea and appetite changes to rare but serious complications, we break down the science behind these medications and share practical tips to manage side effects.

Ozempic (semaglutide) is a medication primarily used to manage type 2 diabetes and, in some cases, for weight loss. While it is effective, like any medication, it carries potential side effects and risks. Below is a comprehensive overview:

Common Side Effects

These are typically mild and may resolve as your body adjusts to the medication:
1.Gastrointestinal Issues
•Nausea (most common, especially early in treatment)
•Vomiting
•Diarrhea
•Constipation
•Abdominal pain or discomfort
2.Appetite Changes
•Decreased appetite (can lead to weight loss)
•Feeling full quickly
3.Fatigue
•Some users report feeling more tired than usual.
4.Injection Site Reactions
•Redness, swelling, or irritation at the injection site.

Serious Side Effects

Though rare, these require immediate medical attention:
1.Thyroid Tumors
•In animal studies, semaglutide has been linked to thyroid C-cell tumors. The FDA advises against its use in individuals with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2.
2.Pancreatitis
•Symptoms include severe abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting.
3.Kidney Damage
•Prolonged dehydration (from nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea) can worsen kidney function.
4.Gallbladder Issues
•Increased risk of gallstones or cholecystitis (inflammation of the gallbladder).
5.Low Blood Sugar (Hypoglycemia)
•More likely if combined with other diabetes medications, such as insulin or sulfonylureas.
6.Allergic Reactions
•Rare but can include rash, itching, swelling, or difficulty breathing.

Potential Risks
1.Weight Loss Concerns
•Excessive weight loss can lead to malnutrition or muscle loss if not managed carefully.
2.Cardiovascular Risks
•Though Ozempic has shown benefits for heart health in many studies, some individuals may experience increased heart rate.
3.Mental Health Changes
•Rare reports of mood swings, depression, or suicidal thoughts in patients.
4.Impact on Digestion
•Slows gastric emptying, which can interfere with the absorption of other medications.

Who Should Avoid Ozempic?
1.Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).
2.Individuals with a history of pancreatitis.
3.Those with severe gastrointestinal disease, such as gastroparesis.
4.Pregnant or breastfeeding individuals (safety not well established).

Monitoring and Safety Tips
•Start Low, Go Slow: Begin with the lowest dose and increase gradually as directed by your healthcare provider to minimize side effects.
•Stay Hydrated: Prevent dehydration, especially if experiencing nausea or vomiting.
•Regular Monitoring: Keep track of blood sugar, kidney function, and weight.
•Healthy Diet: Ensure adequate nutrition, especially if using Ozempic for weight loss.
•Report Symptoms: Inform your doctor of any persistent or severe side effects.

Conclusion

Ozempic is a powerful medication for managing diabetes and weight, but it comes with potential side effects and risks. Close monitoring by a healthcare provider and patient awareness are key to minimizing adverse effects while maximizing benefits. If you’re considering or already taking Ozempic, discuss your medical history and concerns with your doctor.

GLP-1 receptor agonists (like Ozempic, Wegovy, and Mounjaro) are widely prescribed for type 2 diabetes and weight loss. While effective for blood sugar and appetite control, they come with serious potential risks that are often overlooked.

⸻

•Animal studies have shown that GLP-1 drugs can stimulate C-cell growth in the thyroid, leading to tumors.
•The FDA requires a “black box warning” for all GLP-1 medications due to risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC).
•Human studies are still ongoing, but caution is advised — especially in people with a family history of thyroid cancer.

⸻

🔹 2. Kidney Damage & Failure
•GLP-1 drugs can cause severe dehydration due to nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
•This can reduce blood flow to the kidneys, leading to acute kidney injury.
•Case reports have linked GLP-1 use to worsening chronic kidney disease and, in rare cases, kidney failure.

⸻

🔹 3. What You Should Know
•These risks don’t affect everyone, but they are real enough to warrant caution.
•Patients with kidney disease, thyroid nodules, or family history of MTC should discuss alternatives with their doctors.
•Lifestyle changes (nutrition, strength training, circadian health) remain the safest, long-term tools for weight loss and metabolic health.

I’ll clarify the safety, side effects, warnings, precautions, and effectiveness for these drugs.

Safety

Zepbound (tirzepatide): 
The FDA approved Zepbound in November 2023 for adults with obesity (BMI ≥30) or overweight (BMI ≥27) with weight-related conditions like hypertension, type 2 diabetes, or cardiovascular disease, when used with a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity. Its safety profile is consistent with other GLP-1 receptor agonists, showing no major red flags in clinical trials when used as directed. 

However, it carries a boxed warning for the risk of thyroid C-cell tumors, including medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), based on animal studies. No human cases have been confirmed, but the risk cannot be ruled out.

Orforglipron:      
This oral GLP-1 drug is still experimental, with Phase 3 trial results reported in 2025 but no FDA approval yet. Trials indicate a safety profile similar to injectable GLP-1s, with no observed liver damage—a concern that      derailed competitors like Pfizer’s oral GLP-1 candidate. 

However, about 10.3% of participants on the highest dose (36 mg) discontinued due to side effects, compared to 2.6% on placebo, suggesting tolerability issues for some.

General Context: 
Posts on X and some web sources express skepticism about GLP-1 drugs, citing concerns like muscle loss (up to 40% of weight lost may be muscle) or insufficient long-term safety data (beyond 5 years). Side Effects

Zepbound:
Common (≥5% of trial participants): 
Nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, constipation, abdominal pain, dyspepsia (indigestion), injection-site reactions,       fatigue, hypersensitivity reactions, burping, hair loss, and gastroesophageal reflux disease. These are typically mild to moderate and occur most often during dose escalation, decreasing over time.

Discontinuation:       
Gastrointestinal side effects led to higher dropout rates compared to placebo, with some patients stopping treatment due to severity.

Orforglipron:
Common:

Warnings and Precautions

Zepbound:
Boxed Warning: 
Risk of thyroid C-cell tumors (MTC). Contraindicated in patients  with personal or family history of MTC or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2). Symptoms to watch for include neck lump/swelling, hoarseness, or trouble swallowing.

Not safe with other GLP-1 receptor agonists or       tirzepatide-containing products. Unknown safety in patients with prior pancreatitis or children under 18. Precautions:       
Patients should inform healthcare providers of thyroid issues, allergies, or pregnancy (not studied in pregnant women). Gradual dose escalation is used to minimize GI side effects.

Orforglipron:

Warnings:

Oligodendrocytes (OLs) in the median eminence (ME) of the hypothalamus express glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptors (GIPR).

Ozempic (semaglutide), a GLP-1 receptor agonist used primarily for type 2 diabetes and weight loss, has several potential risks and side effects. Here's a concise overview of its dangers based on available information:

### Common Side Effects
- **Gastrointestinal Issues**: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, and abdominal pain are frequent, affecting up to 40% of users, especially during initial treatment or dose escalation. These often subside but can persist in some cases.
- **Injection Site Reactions**: Redness, swelling, or irritation at the injection site.

### Serious Risks
- **Pancreatitis**: A rare but serious risk, with symptoms like severe abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Studies suggest a potential increase in pancreatitis risk, though data is not conclusive.
- **Gallbladder Disease**: Increased risk of gallstones and cholecystitis, particularly with rapid weight loss. Clinical trials report a 1-2% incidence of gallbladder-related events.
- **Thyroid Tumors**: Animal studies showed an increased risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) with GLP-1 agonists. Human risk is unclear, but Ozempic carries a boxed warning for those with a personal or family history of MTC or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2.
- **Kidney Issues**: Rare cases of acute kidney injury, often linked to dehydration from vomiting or diarrhea.
- **Hypoglycemia**: More common in patients also taking insulin or sulfonylureas, with severe low blood sugar events reported in 0.5-2% of users in trials.
- **Allergic Reactions**: Rare but potentially severe, including anaphylaxis or angioedema.

### Long-Term Concerns
- **Muscle Loss**: Rapid weight loss may lead to significant muscle mass reduction (up to 40% of weight lost), potentially causing weakness or metabolic issues.
- **Weight Regain**: Discontinuing Ozempic often leads to weight regain, with studies showing 60-70% of lost weight returning within a year without lifestyle changes.
- **Mental Health**: Emerging reports link GLP-1 agonists to mood changes, including depression or suicidal thoughts, though evidence is limited and under investigation.
- **Cancer Risk**: Beyond thyroid tumors, some studies suggest a potential link to other cancers (e.g., pancreatic), but data is inconclusive and requires further research.

### Specific Populations
- **Pregnancy**: Not recommended due to potential fetal harm based on animal studies. Women are advised to stop Ozempic at least 2 months before planning pregnancy.
- **Elderly**: Increased risk of side effects like dehydration or kidney issues due to age-related physiological changes.

### Practical Considerations
- **Drug Interactions**: May interact with medications affecting gastric emptying or oral absorption, like certain antibiotics or contraceptives.
- **Cost and Access**: High cost (often $900-$1,300/month without insurance) can lead to discontinuation, exacerbating weight regain or diabetes control issues.

### Notes
- Many side effects are dose-dependent and may be mitigated by starting with a low dose and titrating slowly.
- Always consult a healthcare provider to weigh benefits against risks, especially for off-label use like weight loss.

Concerns Emerge Over Potential Cancer Links to Drugs Like Ozempic | Nadine Wehida & Ahmed Elbediwy, The Conversation

So many people in western countries are turning to weight loss drugs such as Wegovy/Ozempic and Mounjaro that concerns have started to emerge about maintaining ready supplies.

But with popularity comes scrutiny, and rising demand isn't the only potential problem with weight loss jabs.

Gastrointestinal side-effects such as nausea, vomiting and constipation are common across these drugs, which are known as GLP-1 receptor agonists. Then there's the now infamous "Ozempic face" – a gaunt, aged appearance that can result from rapid weight loss.

More serious concerns have also begun to surface, including possible links to eye disease, reduced libido and a potential increased risk of certain cancers. However, we're still in the early days of understanding what the risks might be and the evidence for them is limited.

The most significant cancer-related worry is thyroid cancer. Studies in rodents found that high doses of GLP-1 drugs caused thyroid tumors, although this hasn't been definitively proven in humans.

Still, a large-scale French study did find a potential link between GLP-1 use and thyroid cancer, especially in patients who used the drug for more than a year. As a precaution, these medications are not recommended for people with a personal or family history of thyroid cancer or specific genetic conditions that increase the risk of thyroid tumors.

There have also been concerns about pancreatic cancer, mostly because of early reports of pancreatitis: inflammation of the pancreas, which can, in some cases, be fatal. However, current studies have not confirmed a direct link between GLP-1 drugs and pancreatic cancer.

Concerns here are particularly relevant because of how the drugs work.

Wegovy and Ozempic are brand names for a type of GLP-1 receptor agonist known as semaglutide. Originally developed to treat type 2 diabetes, it works by activating receptors in the pancreas to increase insulin release and reduce glucagon – a hormone that raises blood sugar.

Together, these effects help lower blood-sugar levels. The weight loss effects come from the drug's ability to act on receptors in the brain as well as in gut and fat cells, to help to reduce appetite.

Mounjaro (the brand name for the compound tirzepatide) takes things a step further. It works not only on the GLP-1 receptor but also on a second one – the GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide) receptor.

By stimulating both, tirzepatide boosts the pancreas's ability to produce insulin and improves insulin sensitivity – meaning the body's cells respond more effectively to insulin, helping regulate blood sugar more efficiently. This dual action results in even greater weight loss than semaglutide alone, making Mounjaro the latest star in the fight against obesity.

Tirzepatide has not been associated with increased cancer risk in clinical trials so far. However, like other GLP-1 drugs, it still carries the thyroid cancer warning based on earlier animal research.

Interestingly, preliminary studies in animals suggest tirzepatide might even shrink certain tumors, including breast cancer, but these findings are still very early and not yet applicable to humans.

Obesity is also a cancer risk

It's important to remember that obesity itself is a well established risk factor for several cancers, including breast, colon, liver and uterine cancers. By helping people lose significant amounts of weight and improve their metabolic health, GLP-1 drugs could indirectly reduce the risk of developing these conditions.

In fact, some population studies have found lower rates of obesity-related cancers in people using GLP-1 medications compared to those taking other treatments.

However, it's still unclear whether the reduced cancer risk comes from the drug's action or from the weight loss itself. More research is needed to fully understand this connection.

So, the current picture is reassuring, yet tinged with uncertainty. The overall cancer risk associated with GLP-1 drugs and tirzepatide appears to be low.

But it's important to emphasize that these medications are not recommended for people with a personal or family history of certain types of thyroid cancer, or also endocrine conditions such as multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome, because these conditions may increase sensitivity to hormone-related tumor growth.

Weight-loss injections are not risk free, but they also hold enormous potential. It remains to be unraveled whether they're miracle cures or just the latest chapter in the long saga of weight loss.

One thing is certain: the conversation is far from over.

These drugs are rewriting the rules on how we think about weight, health, and risk. In the battle to outsmart the scales, they offer hope, science and a fair bit of gamble amidst the hype.

The Trump administration is planning a pilot program to cover “miracle” weight loss drugs under the government health insurance systems for low-income people and retirees, Medicaid and Medicare, in a move aimed at tackling the US’s chronic obesity problem.

Insurance coverage for such drugs is currently typically approved when patients have other conditions that are often tied to obesity, such as diabetes, heart disease and cancer.

The new proposed plan would permit state Medicaid programs and Medicare Part D insurance plans to voluntarily cover GLP-1 drugs, including those from the market leaders Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly, the report said.

Byproducts from gut bacteria breaking down tryptophan, a dietary amino acid, can restore hormone-secreting gut cells reduced by obesity, a new study found. It opens the door to a natural, side-effect-free alternative to GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic.

Specialized gut cells called enteroendocrine cells (EECs) secrete important hormones such as glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), which help regulate insulin production and appetite. Yes, it’s the GLP-1 that drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy mimic.

New research by scientists from Marshall University, West Virginia, has uncovered how obesity significantly reduces the number of EECs, leading to metabolic dysfunction. They also found that byproducts produced by gut bacteria when they break down certain amino acids can restore them.

“Our findings suggest that microbial metabolites derived from dietary tryptophan can reverse obesity-associated reductions in hormone-secreting cells,” said Alip Borthakur, PhD, assistant professor at Marshall University’s Joan C. Edwards School of Medicine (JCESOM) and the study’s senior author. “This points to a potential therapeutic strategy that leverages gut microbes to improve metabolic outcomes in obesity.”

...

Tryptophan is an essential amino acid, meaning that the body can’t make it, and we need to get it from our diet. It plays a crucial role in making proteins and is a precursor to several important molecules, including serotonin and melatonin (presumably where the sleepy claim came from, although that has been confirmed to be a myth). Studies have shown that when gut bacteria break down tryptophan, one of the byproducts that’s produced is indole. Indole is known to regulate the gut’s immune response by activating the transcription factor aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR). Transcription factors are proteins that bind to DNA and regulate gene expression.

The researchers induced obesity in rats by feeding them a high-fat diet and then measured EEC levels via chromogranin A (CHGA), a marker for EECs, and levels of transcription factors that guide stem cells to become EECs. They treated human gut organoids, “mini organs” grown from healthy human colon tissue, with indole and with Lactobacillus acidophilus bacteria grown with and without tryptophan, to mimic bacterial metabolite exposure. To confirm if AhR played a role, they added an AhR antagonist called CH-223191 to block its function and measured whether it reversed the effects of indole and tryptophan metabolites.

In the obese rats, the researchers found that CHGA levels and EEC numbers dropped by around 60%. Important transcription factors for EEC differentiation were also significantly lowered. Fewer GLP-1-producing cells were found in the obese rats. In the human organoids, indole treatment significantly increased CHGA mRNA and protein, suggesting it promoted EEC formation. L. acidophilus grown with tryptophan caused a greater increase in CHGA than L. acidophilus grown without it. Blocking AhR with CH-223191 prevented these increases, confirming that AhR activation is required for the EEC-boosting effect.

Managing Adverse Effects of Incretin-Based Medications for Obesity
(JAMA Insights, July 2025)
🔑 Background

Incretin-based therapies (GLP-1RA: Semaglutide; GIP/GLP-1RA: Tirzepatide) → revolutionized obesity care.

Benefits: Weight reduction, T2DM control, ↓ cardiovascular & renal risk, improved OSA outcomes.

Challenge: Adverse Effects (AEs) often limit adherence → 6–10% discontinuation in RCTs; ~53% at 1-year in real-world.

🔑 Common GI Adverse Effects

Incidence: Nausea (33–44%), Diarrhea (23–31%), Vomiting (11–25%), Constipation (17–23%), Dyspepsia (9–10%).

Timing: Within 48 hours of initiation or after dose escalation.

Mitigation Strategies:

Start low & slow (semaglutide 0.25 mg → titrate monthly to 2.4 mg; tirzepatide 2.5 mg → up to 15 mg).

Dietary: Small, frequent meals; avoid high-fat foods, alcohol, carbonated drinks.

Supportive Rx:

Ondansetron for nausea/vomiting.

H₂ blockers / PPIs for dyspepsia.

Fiber, hydration, psyllium, docusate, or PEG for constipation.

If persistent: Slow titration, dose reduction, or switch therapy.

🔑 Nutritional & Lifestyle Guidance

Appetite suppression → risk of inadequate nutrition.

Focus on diet quality (not just calorie restriction):

Lean proteins (fish, poultry, legumes, egg whites, low-fat dairy).

Healthy fats (nuts, avocado, olive oil, fatty fish).

Vegetables, fruits, whole grains.

Exercise: Aerobic + resistance training → preserve lean mass, bone health, and functional capacity.

Team-based care: Refer to dietitian, exercise specialist, psychologist as needed.

🔑 Missed Doses & Procedures

Stop 1–2 weeks prior to procedures with anesthesia (delayed gastric emptying risk).

If ≥2 doses missed → restart at lower dose, titrate cautiously.

Extra caution in CKD, prior severe GI AEs, or prolonged interruption.

🔑 Monitoring Weight Loss, Malnutrition & Sarcopenia

Expected average weight loss:

Semaglutide: ~15%

Tirzepatide: ~21%

Warning signs:

Weight loss >5% per month.

<5% loss after 3 months.

Elderly (≥65 years): High risk of sarcopenia & bone loss.

Screening tools:

5 sit-to-stand test, grip strength, knee extensor strength.

Prevention:

≥1.3 g/kg/day protein.

Resistance training ≥2 days/week.

Adjust meds if sarcopenia suspected.

🔑 Long-Term Management

Obesity = chronic disease → requires lifelong therapy.

Stopping GLP-1/GIP drugs:

Often → ↑ hunger & regain ~⅔ of lost weight in 1 year.

↑ risk of recurrent diabetes, HTN, dyslipidemia.

Strategies for sustainability:

Individualized dosing (not always max dose).

Consider reducing frequency or switching to affordable alternatives.

Intensify lifestyle interventions if tapering therapy.

Shared decision-making essential: Balance efficacy, tolerability, cost, and patient goals.

💡 CME INDIA Take-Home

> “GLP-1RA and GIP/GLP-1RA are game-changers in obesity care, but GI AEs, nutritional risks, and sarcopenia require vigilant monitoring. Lifelong, individualized, team-based care is the key to sustainable weight loss and improved outcomes.”

⚡ Practice Pearls

✅ Start low, titrate slow – prevents GI dropout.

✅ Always check protein intake & resistance training in older adults.

✅ For persistent GI issues → think dose adjustment before discontinuation.

✅ Monitor mental health, functional capacity, and sarcopenia risk each visit.

✅ Weight regain post-discontinuation is common → counsel patients early.

🔍 Overview

GLP-1 receptor agonists (e.g., semaglutide/Ozempic, tirzepatide/Mounjaro) have transformed obesity and diabetes care. However, emerging reports highlight a spectrum of oral health complications potentially linked to these agents.

🧪 Key Mechanisms Behind Oral Issues

FactorEffect

Reduced Saliva Production
GLP-1 agonists alter GI secretions, including salivary glands, leading to dry mouth (xerostomia).
Dehydration
Appetite suppression leads to reduced fluid intake; compounded dehydration further decreases salivary flow.
Ketosis
Common in those on calorie-restricted or low-carb diets while on GLP-1; causes fruity “acetone-like” bad breath.
Vomiting
Seen in ~25% of users; causes enamel erosion and acid damage if persistent.

Neglected Oral Hygiene
Reduced appetite may reduce perceived need for oral care and water intake.

🧾 Common Oral Symptoms Reported

Xerostomia (Dry mouth)

Halitosis (Bad breath)

Gingivitis/Periodontitis

Tooth sensitivity

Dental caries/tooth decay

Enamel erosion post-vomiting.
